message: This opener says nothing the reader came for.
fix: Delete it and start with the point.

message: This heading looks like title case: two or more words after the first are capitalized. Proper nouns and acronyms stay capitalized, so check that the capitals are names.
fix: Capitalize only the first word, proper nouns, and the first word after a colon.

message: This phrase means the same as a shorter one. Every word should do work.
fix: Use the short form from the guide's table.

message: The guide addresses the reader directly as "you". "The user" puts a third person between the product and the reader.
fix: Rewrite to "you" ("You get an email when someone assigns you a task"). Use "user" only as a category word, such as "user permissions", or in developer documentation where it means the end user of the reader's software.

message: "Select" works for every input method. Keys are still pressed.
fix: Use "select" for options, values, links, menu items, and buttons.

message: House style uses "sign in" as the verb and "sign-in" as the noun. A swap that would rename an existing UI label everywhere is a product decision, so flag that case rather than changing one screen.
fix: Use "sign in" for the action and "sign-in" for the noun or adjective.

message: Advice phrased as a wish or as the company's opinion is longer and softer than a command. The guide reserves "we" for times when the company must be the speaker, such as a privacy notice or an outage update.
fix: Give the instruction as a command: "Back up the database before you upgrade."

message: The guide spells it as one word with no hyphen.
fix: Write "email".

message: The guide prefers the short, common word. "Enable" stays when it means turn on.
fix: Replace with the plain word. For "via", choose "through", "by", or "using" to fit the sentence.

message: These words add emphasis but no fact. Inside a quotation or a product name they stay.
fix: Delete the word, unless the sentence then loses a fact.

message: This word makes a claim without a fact behind it. Say what the product does instead.
fix: Delete it, or replace it with a concrete statement of behavior.

message: Readers and translation tools misread Latin abbreviations.
fix: Write "for example", "that is", or name the items. For "etc.", prefer "such as" before the list, or say what is included.

message: The em dash is the strongest machine-written tell, and every job it does has a clearer replacement. A double hyphen is treated as an em dash in Markdown.
fix: For an aside, use a pair of commas or parentheses. To introduce a list, use a colon. To join two statements, use a period and two sentences.

message: A sentence that needs a semicolon is usually two sentences or a list.
fix: Split the sentence, or turn the series into a list.

message: An exclamation point reads as shouting in an error and as gushing in a success message.
fix: End the sentence with a period.

message: Curly quotation marks and apostrophes usually come from a word processor. They don't render the same everywhere, and they break copied values.
fix: Replace with the straight character: " or '.

message: Curly quotation marks and apostrophes usually come from a word processor. They don't render the same everywhere, and they break copied values.
fix: Replace with the straight character: " or '.

message: A slash asks the reader to guess whether you mean "and", "or", or both. Fixed pairs such as on/off and read/write are fine.
fix: Write "or" (or "and"). "And/or" almost always means "or".

message: A "was done by" sentence hides the actor at the end. The guide converts to active only when the actor is named or obvious, and keeps passive when it keeps blame off the reader or when the receiver is the point. Only passives with an explicit "by" are flagged.
fix: Put the actor first: "The scheduler generates the report every Monday."

message: Product behavior that happens every time is described in the present tense. A real statement about timing ("will be available in the next release") is a fact and stays.
fix: Use the present tense: "the dialog closes".

message: A feature guide that describes a planned feature becomes a promise. The guide moves such statements to release notes or a roadmap. This is a flag for the author, not an edit.
fix: Flag it: is this released? If not, move it to the release notes or the roadmap.

message: This gives the product a mind. The guide treats it as a claim for the author to confirm, not a style edit.
fix: Flag it for the author and suggest a verb such as ranks, selects, estimates, predicts, or recommends.

message: An unqualified promise is one the product can't keep, because results depend on the customer's data and configuration. This is a claim for the author, not a style edit.
fix: Flag it. Suggest a plain statement of what the product does, or a verb such as ranks, selects, estimates, predicts, or recommends.

message: In prose, counts below 10 are words. Numerals stay for measurements, durations, times, versions, percentages, identifiers, and when a sentence mixes numbers of the same kind above and below 10.
fix: Write the word: "five projects".

message: A numeric date reads differently in different countries. ISO dates belong in data formats, logs, and code.
fix: Write "June 12, 2026".

message: The ordinal suffix adds nothing to a date.
fix: Write "June 1".

message: The unit is a separate word, and the percent sign is not.
fix: Write "25 MB" and "30 ms". In running text, write a percentage as "87 percent".

message: In running text the guide spells out "percent". The symbol is for UI strings and tables.
fix: Write "50 percent".

message: The guide writes times as a numeral, a space, and AM or PM in capitals. Noon and midnight are written as words.
fix: Write "10:45 AM", "noon", or "midnight".

message: A season names different months in each hemisphere.
fix: Name the month or the quarter: "in March" or "in Q1 2027".

message: The guide replaces this term. A term that's part of a command, a setting, or an API stays as written, so flag that case for the product team instead of editing the prose.
fix: Use the replacement from the table.

message: A generic person, such as "the admin" or "a reviewer", gets no gendered pronoun. Gendered pronouns are right only for a named person who uses them and in direct quotations.
fix: In order of preference: rewrite to "you", rewrite to a plural, use "the" or "a", name the role, or use singular "they".

message: The guide's table gives a gender-neutral word for this one.
fix: Use the replacement from the table.

message: Combat language makes an ordinary action sound violent and translates badly. A technical term such as the `kill` command stays as written.
fix: Use the plain word from the guide's table.

message: Focus on people, not conditions, and don't borrow a disability as a metaphor.
fix: Use the plain replacement. "The outage crippled the service" becomes "The outage stopped the service."

message: Politeness words add length and, in an error, sound like blame or panic. Say what happened and what to do.
fix: Delete the word and lead with the action.

message: A confirmation names the object and the consequence so the reader knows what they're deciding.
fix: Name the action and the object: "Delete this project? Its tasks move to your default project."

message: A generic error gives the reader nothing to act on. If the cause is known, name it and say what to do.
fix: Write one message per known cause: what happened, why if the reader can act on it, and what to do next.

message: "Here" tells the reader nothing about where the link goes, and screen readers list links by their text.
fix: Name the destination or the result: "View the sharing rules."

message: Position breaks when the layout changes or a screen reader reads the page in order.
fix: Name the section and link to it, or name the control.

message: A screen reader already announces that this is an image.
fix: Describe what the image shows or does: "The Sharing tab with Invite people selected."

message: Each step in a numbered procedure is a full sentence and ends with a period.
fix: Add the period.

message: List items start with a capital letter, even when they're fragments. A code value or identifier that must stay lowercase is the exception, and it belongs in code style.
fix: Capitalize the first word, or put a lowercase identifier in code style.

message: A list item stands on its own. Trailing punctuation or conjunctions turn the list back into a sentence.
fix: Remove the trailing semicolon, comma, or conjunction.

message: A blank cell could mean none, not applicable, or forgotten.
fix: Write "None" or "Not applicable". If you don't know which, flag it.

message: Symbols in a heading read as abbreviations and don't translate.
fix: Write "and".

message: These connectors stitch paragraphs together without adding a fact. Each paragraph should stand on its own first sentence.
fix: Delete the connector. If the paragraphs need a link, make it a fact.

message: The brand table in the guide gives the owner's casing. Only the brands the guide itself prints are checked. Add your own rows to this rule when you fill in the brand table.
fix: Use the casing from the brand table.

message: "(s)" asks the reader to parse two sentences at once and breaks screen readers.
fix: Write "one or more files", or use the plural.

message: Headings and labels take no end punctuation other than a question mark.
fix: Remove the period or ellipsis.
